title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishesByJaroslav LukivNearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousan
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishesByJaroslav LukivNearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on SaturdayClashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.Image source, EPAImage caption, Protesters clash with police at a demonstration in BordeauxIn the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture."There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.Image caption, "We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBCEarlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office."They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government."I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".Image source, ReutersMeanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully.Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.Image source, EPAImage caption, People clash with police during a demonstration against the high cost of living in Bordeaux.Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

schema.headline: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France

title: UK weather: Amber warnings kick in as Storm Boelo to bring 80mph wind gusts
description: The National Grid said on Saturday that more than 124,000 properties had been restored with power supplies since the beginning of the storm. However,
body: The National Grid said on Saturday that more than 124,000 properties had been restored with power supplies since the beginning of the storm. However, hundreds were still without power on Saturday evening.In north-west England, more than 2,000 properties were without power on Saturday night due to the storm.Strong winds could cause power cuts, flying debris, damage to buildings and trees, travel disruption and danger to life from large waves, the Met Office said.The strongest winds affected western Scotland first, and are expected to spread eastwards overnight and through Sunday.By Saturday evening, wind gusts of 75mph had been reached at South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland, on Saturday, according to the Met Office.Train and ferry services have been cancelled in Scotland and police have warned against unnecessary road journeys. Dozens of flood warnings and alerts were in place across the country and flooding also closed a number of roads, including the A78 Inverkip Road in Greenock; the A77 at Lendalfoot in Ayrshire; and several in Dumfries and Galloway.It has emerged that an oil tanker sailing 350 nautical miles off the Isle of Mull with 21 people on board issued a distress alert to the HM Coastguard because of "large swells" on Saturday afternoon."A Royal Air Force (RAF) aircraft was sent to investigate and established communications with the vessel," a spokesperson for the UK's Coastal & Maritime Agency said in a statement, without detailing from which country the ship was flagged. The statement continued: "It was determined that there was no need for assistance, and that the vessel would continue with onwards passage."Events across the country planned for this weekend have been cancelled due to the weather, and a number of travel disruptions have been reported.In Merseyside, a River of Light event has been called off for the second day in a row, and Knowsley Safari Park has announced that it will close on Sunday due to "high winds". Several markets across the North West have also been cancelled due to the weather, including Quayside Makers Market in Salford and Macclesfield Treacle Market in Cheshire. Dublin Airport in Ireland has cancelled several outbound and inbound flights and ferry providers such as StenaLine, Irish Ferries and P&O Ferries have cancelled a number of ferry crossings in the Irish Sea. Jason Kelly, the Met Office's chief forecaster, said: "People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies. Secure loose items outside, plan ahead if you are travelling and keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings for your area."

schema.headline: UK weather: Amber warnings kick in as Storm Boelo to bring 80mph wind gusts

title: Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'
description: Image source, Aaron Chown - WPA Pool/Getty ImagesByDaniela RelphSenior royal correspondentRoyal tours are unpredictable beasts.The planning is meticul
body: Image source, Aaron Chown - WPA Pool/Getty ImagesByDaniela RelphSenior royal correspondentRoyal tours are unpredictable beasts.The planning is meticulous and dates back months, sometimes years, but there is always jeopardy.King Charles III's visit to the Caribbean, which starts on Tuesday, takes him to three countries in nine days: the Bahamas, Guyana and finally Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).It also throws him directly into the heat of the debate over the payment of reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade - alongside questions of whether the King should be apologising for the UK's role in what he has previously described as an "appalling atrocity" that leaves an "indelible stain" on history."This is the biggest risk of his reign so far with so much just outside of his control," said author and historian Sir Anthony Seldon. "Questions about slavery, reparations and apologies mean the moral integrity of the monarchy is being questioned."The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade. A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government. The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022. Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.Image source, Chris Jackson-Pool/Getty ImagesImage caption, The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge shook hands with children through a wire fence during a visit to Trench Town on their 2022 tour Image source, Toby Melville - Pool / Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman holds a sign in protest as she waits for the arrival of William and Catherine on their tour  The leadership in the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda will celebrate the King and his work in protecting rainforests, creating cultural ties and reinforcing relationships around trade, energy, and agriculture.But they do so against a backdrop of change.The leaders of all three countries have voiced their support for reparatory justice.In Antigua and Barbuda and the Bahamas, where the King is head of state, the conversation about becoming a republic has significant support.Elected officials in the former no longer have to pledge allegiance to the King ending a 40-year tradition of swearing loyalty to the monarch."He pulled off an extraordinary triumph with President Trump in his US visit earlier this year and stood up to him and put him in his place in a way that no leader has done - while not incurring his wrath," said Sir Anthony. "If he can deal with the delicate nature of this trip for him personally, for the British monarchy, and the future of the Commonwealth, it could be an enormous success."The Sussexes surprise return Timing also matters for royal tours.This Caribbean tour has to cut through a sea of royal distractions.The King has spent much of the past three months in Scotland, where he is based over the summer.It should have been a quieter time in the royal calendar, but it has been quite the opposite.The surprise return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to the UK has been noisy. The level of coverage Harry and Meghan get is unsettling and, at times, irritating for the Royal Family.The King's youngest son has not yet seen his father in person, but they are said to have talked.Then enter Earl Spencer, the King's former brother-in-law, with his memoir, Swan Song, criticising the King's response to the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. It triggered a strong pushback from the Palace.And in recent days, the serious claims made about Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, have drawn his daughter into a complex tale involving global police forces, sexual abuse allegations and further family trauma.An impactful and successful Caribbean tour is a chance to switch focus.But if royal stories back home are running hot, it can be hard to focus minds on the King's engagements over four thousand miles (6,437km) away.Image source, Mark Cuthbert/Getty ImagesImage caption,  Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has received a lot of coverage Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy, who has strong family ties to the Caribbean, has accompanied the King on a number of trips outside the UK."He is our head of state. He is amongst some of the most recognisable figures in the world. For a small country like Guyana, the validation of a state visit is huge," said the Tottenham MP whose father came to the UK from what was then British Guiana and who also has relatives in Antigua and Barbuda. "My mother would forever recall the Queen's visit in 1996."But there was also a recognition of that royal trip jeopardy."Knowing Guyana, Antigua and Barbuda as well as I do, he will be overwhelmingly received positively," Lammy said. "But these are lively democracies in which of course there will be some dissent."A transatlantic flight, three countries over nine days and about 36 separate engagements when you're closing in on your 78th birthday is an intense schedule. It is also a reminder that the King is still dealing with a cancer diagnosis and having regular treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated its position that he is on a "positive trajectory".Queen Camilla will only accompany the King on the Antigua and Barbuda leg of the visit for Chogm and a number of other engagements, including some around her own areas of interest – literacy and supporting efforts to end violence against women and girls.The Queen, who will be 80 next July, is known to find the pace and hot conditions of some royal tours gruelling.This is a trip that comes with potential pitfalls but also the possibility of great reward for the King."The King can be an extraordinarily empathetic and in tune figure," Sir Anthony said."He could play a blinder here."Additional reporting by Felicity BakerRelated topicsKing Charles IIIUK Royal FamilyPrince William, Prince of WalesCatherine, Princess of WalesThe Royal Family and the mediaPrince Harry, Duke of SussexMeghan, Duchess of SussexCaribbeanSlavery

schema.headline: Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'

title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents
description: Image source, Eddie LeverImage caption, Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights ActByBecky MortonPolitica
body: Image source, Eddie LeverImage caption, Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights ActByBecky MortonPolitical reporterWhen the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.Eddie Lever had finished his first year at the University of Exeter when he decided the course wasn't for him.The 20-year-old wanted to switch to studying international relations at the University of York but had already organised his house for the upcoming year.The tenancy was signed and had started.But because of changes in the Renters' Rights Act, Eddie only had to give two months' notice before he could leave and stop paying rent.The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months. For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.Instead, properties are now rented on a rolling basis, which means tenants pay rent weekly or monthly with no fixed end date.University-owned halls of residence and Purpose-Built Student Accommodation are exempt, external and can still offer fixed-term contracts so this change primarily affects students renting from a private landlord."If the Renters' Rights Act wasn't a thing, I don't think I would have been able to move universities because I would have been locked into the full [year] contract," Eddie explains."It would have made it unaffordable."As he was signed up to a joint tenancy, when he left it ended the tenancy for the whole house.Fortunately, Eddie had a friend who was looking for a room who was able to take his place so his housemates could sign a new tenancy.He acknowledges the situation would have been more difficult for his housemates if there wasn't someone who could take his room.However, Eddie thinks the benefits for students are worth this risk."If you were to fall out with your flatmates or if you decide that university is not for you, being locked into a full-term contract can be really prohibitive financially," he says."So without that flexibility, people can really be locked into situations that they don't necessarily want to be in."Lewis Wilson, vice president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says this flexibility means students can also save money on rent by moving home for the summer.While previously, many student rental contracts ran into the summer after courses had finished, students can now choose to move out earlier if they want.Wilson says students also benefit from wider changes in the act, which bans landlords in England from evicting tenants without a reason.Campaigners argue this gives renters greater security and confidence to ask for repairs, without fearing they could be evicted if they raise concerns.Image source, NUSImage caption, Lewis Wilson from the NUS says the legislation has given students more freedom to move out when they wantHowever, greater flexibility for students to leave tenancies also means less certainty for landlords.The act did introduce a specific ground, external for landlords to evict a group of students at the end of the academic year if they intend to re-let the property to students.Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association, says the bigger problem for student landlords is if their tenants choose to move out earlier.He argues this is a bigger risk for students - who may fall out with their housemates or drop out of university - than, for example, families, who are less likely to want to move out after just a few months.Norris says the end of fixed-term tenancies means student houses could be left empty over the summer after courses finish - or even earlier.He adds that it is now more difficult for student landlords to rent a house for just a few months as they don't know how long the tenants will stay and can't guarantee it will be available for students again in the autumn.Norris says it's early days for the new legislation and many landlords are taking this year as a test to see how these issues play out in practice.However, he warns that some may choose to increase the monthly rent they charge to cover the risk of their properties being empty over the summer.In some cases, he says landlords may even sell up or stop renting to students, reducing supply and pushing up prices.Image source, Sue LawesImage caption, Sue Lawes thinks the changes mean many student landlords will put up their rentSue Lawes, who rents three shared houses to students in Norwich, is worried about the changes.While Sue says she doesn't want to put up her prices, if her houses end up being empty over the summer because students decide to end their tenancy after their final exams she says she may have to.She has already brought forward the start of her tenancy agreements to August instead of September to try and reduce the risks of this.However, she says if her tenants move out earlier in the year she would struggle to make a profit, whilst covering costs including her mortgage, council tax and utility standing charges when the properties are empty.She argues higher monthly rents would mean bigger upfront costs for students and higher overall costs for those who do choose to carry on renting over the summer.Sue stresses that she supports the aim of the legislation to give tenants greater security and that students should be able to move out if their landlord is not carrying out repairs.But she wants landlords to be allowed to offer fixed-term contracts to students in line with the academic year to avoid properties being left empty over the summer."Landlords are going to find it very, very hard to absorb those void periods," she says."Landlords will put prices up and students are going to pay."

schema.headline: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

title: Man Utd not an unmanageable club says boss Michael Carrick
description: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick has dismissed a theory the Old Trafford club are unmanageable.Carrick is clinging on to his job after a d
body: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick has dismissed a theory the Old Trafford club are unmanageable.Carrick is clinging on to his job after a desperate run of seven games without a win before Sunday's Premier League home game against Bournemouth (14:00 GMT).The pressure on him has been heightened by controversial comments from senior players Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes attacking the club's recruitment and his tactics.If Carrick were to lose his job, it would be the third change of manager in as many seasons and mean eight long-term bosses, including Ralf Rangnick, have lost their jobs after failing to get close to the heights of Sir Alex Ferguson, who retired in 2013.Given the pressure on the club is heightened by the number of prominent ex-players who have their own media outlets, and the proliferation of fan channels that attract large numbers of viewers, there is an argument it makes United an impossible club to manage.Carrick had a one-word answer to that notion: "No."However, Carrick does take issue with some of the claims made about his team by former professionals and casual observers.He is vexed at the sense his team do not run enough, and do not press the opposition when they are out of possession.Carrick has accepted the general performance of his team in a 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como on Wednesday was "unacceptable".However, he does not see how claims his team do not press stand up to much scrutiny."You've got to be careful with just saying 'not running'," he said."We've won a lot of games over a period of time and this pressing thing; pressing is one small part of football."There are all sorts of different ways that are classed as a press. What actually is it? What are you doing it for? Is it to your strength? Is it covering up other spaces?"It's just thrown about as a bit of a word at the minute. You don't necessarily need to press to win games of football. Sometimes you do, sometimes you don't."It's not necessarily just running stats that define football games either."We've just got to get back to doing a lot of the things that we were doing last season and for certain parts of this season."Although Carrick was appointed ahead of his former boss and team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer as Ruben Amorim's replacement in January, the pair remain close.Solskjaer drove up to United's base in Trondheim before the pre-season victory over Rosenborg in July to spend time with Carrick and his backroom team.They have been in touch this week, with Carrick also confirming he had spoken to Ferguson, who is a regular at matches as he approaches his 85th birthday.Ferguson signed Carrick from Tottenham in 2006 and also managed the midfielder's Manchester United team in his testimonial game at Old Trafford in 2017."I speak to both of them quite regularly," he said. "There's nothing particular in that. I'm close to both of them. It's nothing different this week."Carrick is convinced he can turn the situation around but knows he needs his underperforming squad to deliver against Bournemouth."I definitely trust them, 100%," he said."We'll be a different team on Sunday. We have to be a different team on Sunday."

schema.headline: Man Utd not an unmanageable club says boss Michael Carrick

title: Donegal: Brown bears adjusting to new life in Irish countryside
description: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and TyapaImage source, Wild Ireland press handoutImage caption, Tyapa (left)
body: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and TyapaImage source, Wild Ireland press handoutImage caption, Tyapa (left) and Bu (right) were previously kept in small cages in the Republic of Dagestan in RussiaByMike McBrideBBC News NIAfter years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people.For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright.Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal.Image caption, Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County DonegalWild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal.The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx.Image caption, Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkableMcLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued.Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform.McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat.The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display.When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma.Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration.How do you transport two large bears?Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin.An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region.More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland.Image source, Wild Ireland press handoutImage caption, The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears.Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine.After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August.Health improvements since arrivingSince arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal.He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy."These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring."We hope they can now have a full and happy life."Working with bears isn't your normal 9-5Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes.Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team."This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said. Image caption, Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job"We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said."Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them."What do visitors think of the bears?Image caption, Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressiveLiam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park."Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa."I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite."Image caption, Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019."I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa."It was fantastic to see them in the flesh."We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."

schema.headline: Donegal: Brown bears adjusting to new life in Irish countryside

title: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strikeByTiffany Werth
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strikeByTiffany WertheimerUkraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation. France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared to Starlink's 10,000-plus.The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death."God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.Figure caption, Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?Why does Starlink dominate in Ukraine?Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks."You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations. Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored, highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate."Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Elon Musk.While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS."This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/ Getty ImagesImage caption, Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefieldStarlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to, agree.Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield," a soldier said.The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones," said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.They are also about five times more expensive, she added.What can the EU offer right now?Rhetoric from the White House - like Donald Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC. She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.Comments from Elon Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted, external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently," a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last yearEva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing, because as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."Iris² - The EU's future networkGovsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris², external is up and running in 2029.The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen."Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".Image source, Paul Hennessy/ Getty ImagesImage caption, A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, carrying 56 Starlink satellites, takes off from Cape Canaveral in MarchA highly-produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity." So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea."Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE, external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences. And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need "a lot of money". Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years. "Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.Why Space is the new defence frontierMilitary work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare."Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels."In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko

schema.headline: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

title: Aston Villa 2-1 Man City: Gianluigi Donnarumma and Marc Guehi under spotlight
description: Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season came to an abrupt end against Aston Villa - leaving Enzo Maresca with glaring defens
body: Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season came to an abrupt end against Aston Villa - leaving Enzo Maresca with glaring defensive issues to resolve.Nicolas Jackson's double in a 2-1 home win for Villa means City have now managed only one clean sheet in their past six games and the form of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma and defender Marc Guehi is of concern.Since the start of last season, only eight players have made more errors leading to Premier League goals than Donnarumma and Guehi with three each.City's most recent shutout came in their impressive victory at Liverpool two weeks ago but, around that game, City have conceded against teams ranging from Champions League holders Paris St-Germain to top-flight strugglers Sunderland.Maresca was forced to try different combinations at the back against Villa, but as the legendary Sir Alex Ferguson once said, "attack wins you games, defence wins you titles".Though still early days in the campaign and guaranteed to be in the top two come the end of the weekend, City need to shore up their backline if they are to stay there.By contrast, title rivals Arsenal moved level on points at the top of the table later in the day with a comfortable 2-0 win at home to Everton.The Gunners have conceded just five goals in eight matches, with Saturday's goals coming from centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel.That's back-to-back Premier League clean sheets for Mikel Arteta's men, with the luxury of centre-back William Saliba still to come back into the side.Only Manchester United - 1.16 in 1996-97 and 1.18 in 1999-00 - have won the Premier League title with a goals against rate worse than Man City's current 1.13 per game. Arsenal's goals against rate is currently 0.625 per game.Asked if the two goals the conceded were avoidable, Maresca told TNT Sports: "Absolutely, both. "Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances, but we created a lot of chances."We played most of the game in their box but you have to be clinical and avoid mistakes like the two goals we conceded."City were undone by goals in each half from the brilliant Jackson at a raucous Villa Park to end their streak of seven straight wins at the start of this campaign.Maresca's team started the season by conceding eight goals in their first nine games but that has seen a dramatic downturn, with nine goals hitting the back of their net in the past four matches.The signing of Donnarumma last summer was heralded as the acquisition of one of the best goalkeepers in the world to replace Ederson.The Brazilian changed the face of English football with his footwork, spraying short and long passes across the pitch, and there are few keepers who can come close to matching that.But Italy captain Donnarumma struggles with the ball at his feet and often puts his team-mates in trouble with passes out from the back.On Saturday, City captain Ruben Dias gesticulated to his team-mate to send the ball up the pitch after the Portuguese failed to control a difficult pass.Maresca decided to sell James Trafford to Leeds for £45m in the summer, and the England international has been impressive at Elland Road.Trafford has made more passes than Donnarumma this season, has a slightly better rate at preventing goals and has come out to sweep the ball 11 times compared with Donnarumma's one.Though Donnarumma could do little about Jackson's thumping finish for the opening goal, he should have done better for the second as a low shot seemed to squirm under him.Former City defender Steph Houghton said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think Villa really utilised keeping the ball and being a real threat to Manchester City. Donnarumma, especially with the second goal, could probably have done a little bit better."But I don't want to take anything away from Villa. I think they performed really, really well and the gameplan was spot on, just to nullify City as much as possible."Centre-back Guehi's £20m arrival from Crystal Palace in January was considered a bargain.But it was his loose pass at Everton late last season which cost City dearly in the title race, drawing that game and losing the impetus to eventual champions Arsenal.This season has been a struggle for the England defender, culpable for both goals scored by Ipswich last weekend and being picked off by John McGinn deep in his own half for Villa's first goal.Later in the half, he hauled down Jackson on the edge of the box before being shown a yellow card, and was put out of his misery by being taken off at half-time.City sources had said they were targeting signing a right-back in the summer before pivoting elsewhere, saying Abdukodir Khusanov can provide back-up should Matheus Nunes not be available.Khusanov started out wide but struggled before being moved inside in place of Guehi, while Rico Lewis was brought to fill the gap, with Maresca acknowledging afterwards he needs to "find that balance" in defence.Villa supporters provided constant reminders to the travelling fans of their side being "cheats", and the vitriol faced following the guilty verdict of the financial charges may be beginning to weigh on the players' minds.Asked by BBC Sport if Guehi's form is a worry, Maresca said: "No, I'm not worried about Marc at all."I know he is playing every minute since the season started with us and the national team, so it's not easy but the change was also because he was on a yellow card."The way we want to be aggressive sometimes, to have one yellow card can be dangerous but I am not worried at all."Maresca, though, should be concerned by coming up against Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring Brighton twice next week - in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, and Premier League on Saturday.The Italian needs to fix the defensive leaks before they become something more serious.

schema.headline: Aston Villa 2-1 Man City: Gianluigi Donnarumma and Marc Guehi under spotlight

title: Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron home
description: The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacin
body: The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacing hundreds of families, according to local officials.Footage shared online showed destruction caused by Israeli bulldozers, with at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened. The military has also cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.The operation was announced by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday, in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.Netanyahu said on Friday that buildings around the site of the attack and the neighbourhoods that the two gunmen were from would be "destroyed".Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which centred on the Ein Deir Baha and Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhoods, and targeted homes, businesses, industrial sites and infrastructure.He said dozens of families had been forced to spend the night outside, with some told to leave without taking their vehicles, while homes were marked for demolition with spray paint.He added that he believed the military planned to displace a total of 2,500 people from about 0.35 sq km of urban land. The city's governor and deputy mayor meanwhile said at least 200 families had been displaced.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond immediately to the BBC's request for comment. It said in a statement on social media that it had dozens of targets across the West Bank and that its operations would last for several days.It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment. Netanyahu likened the operation to previous operations in Palestinian refugee camps in the north of the territory, when the Israeli military demolished hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands in 2025.Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, with Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - cancelled his party's campaign events for Friday morning and headed to Hebron, wearing protective armour and posting a video on social media from the scene."We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons we find there, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure," he said. He also announced he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967 - though did not say when it could be carried out. It is not clear whether the ongoing Hebron operation forms part of that.In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, he threatened "a very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory. In a statement, the PA called for "urgent international action that went beyond condemnation" to prevent further forced displacement.Meanwhile, his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the PA.Speaking to journalists, Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was "driven by the elections," and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far-right and the settlers.

schema.headline: Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron home

title: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas
description: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband saysImage source, SuppliedImage caption, The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island
body: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband saysImage source, SuppliedImage caption, The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of Leanne Gregory on TuesdayByBen CarrEast MidlandsThe husband of a British woman who died rescuing their sons when they were swept away to sea in the Bahamas says she was a "hero... in life and in death".Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been snorkelling with her family when the boys were swept away by a strong current, police said. Although the children were rescued from the water off the island of Bimini on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.Nathan Gregory said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable for our family".'Absolute hero'"She was the purest, most amazing wife, mother and friend to have ever walked this Earth," her husband said in a Facebook post."I will never get over this, she was my soulmate, my childhood sweetheart, my one and only. The foundation of my entire family and the strength that held us all together."My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know Mum died an absolute hero."Gregory said he had also set up a fundraising page "for my sons and security after the tragic loss".In the post on that page he described how his wife, who he had been with for 22 years, had held on to their son until he was rescued "but didn't have the energy to save herself".He added: "I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely."Image source, NurPhoto/Getty ImagesImage caption, The two children were rescued off the coast of Bimini, police in the Bahamas saidIn a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given.Mrs Gregory was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected".A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas."We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Nottingham

schema.headline: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas

title: Tottenham Hotspur: Are Roberto de Zerbi's side finally on their way back after win at Chelsea?
description: Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th
body: Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th in the Premier League - their highest league position since 2 January.And, after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes, there are growing signs Roberto de Zerbi's side are showing there is real light at the end of a pretty dark tunnel.Saturday's impressive win at Stamford Bridge was just the second time they have won two league games in a row in 42 attempts - inspired by starring roles from James Maddison and Mathys Tel.It was also the first time they have enjoyed as much as 68% possession in a match since April 2025.The win was deserved too, although Chelsea certainly gave them a helping hand with goalkeeper Mike Penders punching the opener into his own net and Cole Palmer sent off for two yellow cards.Spurs had taken seven attempts to get their first league win of the season against Coventry on Monday and on Saturday they looked transformed from the side that did not even score a goal until September 1.It left De Zerbi glowing with positivity, despite another injury setback for Maddison, as he highlighted a team meeting earlier this month that sparked their revival in fortunes."Seven points after Manchester. Before Manchester we spoke a lot, we had a big meeting," he said. "We removed the masks and spoke honestly and clearly in front of ourselves. From that moment, I think something started to change within us."I think we have put something different into Tottenham in the last period. Not a different attitude, but different relationships with the players, different relationships within the group."We have changed the spirit of the group and improved the performances of the players, especially some of the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We have suffered enough."Former Chelsea goalkeeper Rob Green added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "A dream afternoon for Tottenham. They looked controlled, looked at ease, they looked like they were comfortable on the ball."Results like this galvanise a side. When you look at the players coming back, yes Maddison got injured and he'll be a question mark over the next few weeks, but players coming back, momentum coming back - you feel, and say it quietly, Tottenham might just be coming back."Italian De Zerbi was appointed Spurs boss at the end of March 2026 with the club in crisis.He arrived as the club's third manager of the campaign and, with seven games remaining, Tottenham were just one point clear of the drop zone.After securing safety, albeit after a few scares, the club spent more than £300m on summer signings for the first time in their history as they backed De Zerbi to restore them to former glories.And, after a slow start to the campaign and still lacking firepower in attack, the long-suffering Tottenham fans will be left feeling more positive than they have done for a long time."Tottenham have made a big statement in a really convincing performance," former Arsenal defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport."I thought Maddison was magnificent in midfield. He's like the Artful Dodger, isn't he? That midfield is full of mischief, but he's brave against the ball."I thought Tel was magnificent out on the left-hand side, [Mohammed] Kudus on the right was also really effective, and everybody really managed to handle the ball really well on the night. "Spurs had almost 70% possession, which is remarkable for a team which was just a few places from the bottom of the table. I think what's changed for Spurs is the key personnel."De Zerbi ran on to the pitch to celebrate with the travelling supporters at the final whistle, while his coaches and substitutes raced towards the players in the corner of the ground.He has previously spoken of how he inherited players that cried after matches and lost all confidence - and believed his unprecedented control over the summer transfers was vindication for Spurs from last season.It was fitting that Tel, who has attracted criticism from his own supporters since arriving from Bayern Munich for £30m in June 2025, provided the decisive moment to seal just a second league success in 36 years at Chelsea - a stunning low finish after a driving run.The French forward, 21, told Sky Sports: "It is very special because we have come to Chelsea so many times and not got a win. We showed great mentality today and we need to enjoy this win."We created a lot of chances today. We walk out together, the goal is something special for me, I'm happy about it and let's keep pushing now."Summer signing Matheus Fernandes added: "We are here to change the club's mentality, we want to beat the top teams, and make this victory for the fans."In the summer, Spurs twice broke their transfer record with three of their first signings, as they added centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton, Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle.And all three impressed De Zerbi against Chelsea as he added: "Jan Paul van Hecke played very well, Matheus Fernandes played very well, Sandro Tonali played very well."I think it was Tonali's best game since joining Tottenham. Omar Marmoush played a good game. It was a tough game for him, but he fought in the right way."Mathys Tel played very well too. I think we won the game with our two wingers, Mohammed Kudus and Mathys Tel. They made the difference."It was notable Fernandes, 22, was criticised by his manager last month.The return of Maddison, who missed almost all of last season with a serious knee injury, was key in Monday's 3-1 home victory over Coventry City - and he again looked impressive before being withdrawn in the second half with a suspected groin injury."I don't think it is a very important problem," said De Zerbi. "I hope it is not a big problem. He is a special player for us. We need him."Maddison is part of a returning group of players, including Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski, who are making comebacks from lengthy absences.Spurs are now unbeaten in three games, with back-to-back victories following the 1-1 draw at Manchester United in which they were arguably the better side.As well as the team meeting before the Old Trafford encounter, Spurs enjoyed a warm-weather training camp in Marbella, where heavyweight boxer Anthony Joshua paid them a visit.It feels as though some semblance of the old Spurs is returning, although they remain unconvincing in attack with just eight goals in as many games.Manchester City loanee Marmoush misfired again and his replacement Dominic Solanke was underwhelming in previous matches, while Richarlison has been frozen out in the reserves after being left out of their Premier League squad.But after this notable derby victory at Chelsea - earning a clean sheet there too for the first time since 1986 - it felt like the first part of De Zerbi's rebuild is well under way.

schema.headline: Tottenham Hotspur: Are Roberto de Zerbi's side finally on their way back after win at Chelsea?

title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
description: The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.Spe
body: The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement."I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now."It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times., external"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it"."Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said."The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch"."He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.

schema.headline: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement

title: Brazil election: Voters to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son
description: Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.Bolsonaro's supporters were
body: Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.Bolsonaro's supporters were jubilant at his final campaign rallies, confident that he would bring change to Brazil through his promised tough crackdown on organised crime, as well as tax and public spending cuts. He campaigned on the eve of polls in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, which has been a must-win state for any presidential hopeful since the 1980s."The time is almost here," Bolsonaro told supporters in a social media video."There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years." He has also pledged to release his father, who is currently serving his sentence under house arrest due to ill health. In Barra de Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, where Jair Bolsonaro has a home, Bolsonaro supporters rallied in support of him dressed in the national colours."Brazil needs change, and Flávio is the person that represents that today, after so many years of the Left destroying the economy and the country," one told BBC News.Another said that what she most liked about Flávio Bolsonaro was his promise to "end violence in Brazil, end terrorism, narco-trafficking, and to reduce interest rates".

schema.headline: Brazil election: Voters to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son

title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
description: Former President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democr
body: Former President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections."This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday.Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America". The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump.Speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House."After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough,'" the former president said in Cleveland. Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy. "If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now".Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were "temporarily high" but said "our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down".The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry "we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs", and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress.He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would "loot your wealth" and "annihilate your borders".Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia - countries which he described as "terror-infested".Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: "I said, 'Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from, like, well... Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'"

title: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs
description: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlistsImage source, Getty Images for iHeartRadioImage caption, One of 2026's biggest hits is
body: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlistsImage source, Getty Images for iHeartRadioImage caption, One of 2026's biggest hits is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, originally released in 2015ByThomas SpencerMore music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services. And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?Old vs new?In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs, external were released 12 months ago, or earlier. The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".It's a similar story in the US.There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, external, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.A 'drought' of new music in the UK Charts?Even when current songs do break out, they themselves dominate streaming for weeks and even months.Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's duet Rein Me In recently made UK chart history, spending a record-breaking 23 non-consecutive weeks at number one.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Olivia Dean and Sam Fender have broken chart history with Rein Me In, after 19 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the UK singles chartWhat about grassroots music?Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song."It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard, external. "For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?" It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation."You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News. "Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.Image source, J CasaImage caption, Rapper J Casa is one of thousands of grassroots artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming platformsIn an age of content oversaturation, Casa thinks there's something unique about a live performance.Rather than hearing more of what they already know, Casa says audiences form "a lasting connection" with a new artist and their music.Sofar is also launching its Human Discovery Movement, external campaign that aims to put music curation and discovery "back into human hands."Music lovers can now text a "mystery number" and receive voice notes from Sofar's tastemakers with recommendations for new music worldwide.Are streaming platforms preaching to the choir?Artificial intelligence (AI) may also be playing its part in the so-called death of new music.Spotify, and its competitors like Apple Music and Amazon Music, are driving the trend in AI-assisted curation, allowing premium subscribers to automatically generate playlists through text prompts to fit a mood, vibe or occasion.Musicologist Anna-Kaisa Kaila thinks "there absolutely is potential for bias" with AI-generative playlist technology."With AI systems, the bias can either come from the data or from the system itself. If there's not enough training data in a particular style that is perhaps not so commercially dominant, it will be that much harder for the system to pull up tracks in that style."Others fear an algorithmic streaming bubble is to the detriment of genuine music, its discovery and creatives' livelihoods.As Tim Garcia, London-based DJ and curator puts it: "They're based on everyone's listening behaviour and data, right? So, you're probably going to get given a very similar recommendation to an artist you're already listening to."Dan Mackta, managing director at Qobuz, an online music platform that maintains a strict human-first approach to curation, agrees the technology "is never going to want to throw a curve ball at you".Image source, Jordan MatykaImage caption, London-based artist Chiminyo performs at his ongoing jazz-electronic NRG projectChiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced."Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies, external against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.
